newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition to end protests.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition to end protests.

text.p: Serbia's opposition has promised to end its marathon street protests when parliament restores its municipal victories next Tuesday but vows to fight on for democracy and free media.
"Democracy has become a way of life. We can no longer live without fighting for democracy," opposition leader Vesna Pesic said on Thursday.
"The moment we get all our mandates back, we shall launch our struggle for free media," she said.

Her two other partners in the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition leadership said the street protests would stop but President Slobodan Milosevic's every move would be closely followed even as the opposition agreed to a dialogue.
"We will stop the protests and will give a chance to dialogue if parliament approves the bill," Vuk Draskovic said in Paris after meeting Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.

Even as the biggest political crisis in Serbia for the last decade appeared to be nearing its end, the Belgrade Board of Deans said the University would be completely shut down as of Monday, independent Radio B92 reported.

A few faculties had continued working throughout the 80-day protests while much of the 80,000-student body in Belgrade staged their own daily demonstrations independent of Zajedno but sharing the same demands.
The biggest challenge to Milosevic's rule started when Zajedno surprisingly won in Serbia's 14 biggest cities, including Belgrade, at the November 17 local elections.
Milosevic's ruling Socialists then annulled the results citing various "irregularities" and prompting massive street protests by the opposition and students and drawing sharp international criticism.
In a sudden reversal earlier this week, Milosevic ordered his parliament on Tuesday to reinstate the disputed results in line with a ruling by an OSCE fact-finding mission in December.
But on arrival from Paris Draskovic warned a Belgrade municipality was missing from a list of Zajedno victories which the Serbian parliament must restore.

Undaunted by police brutality over the weekend, thousands of Zajedno supporters turned up on Thursday evening to attend the main rally in a central Belgrade square after their three leaders returned from Paris.
"You alone have improved Serbia's bad image abroad, you are backed by the French people, the whole world," Draskovic said.
Serbia's image was tarnished abroad during the devastating 43-month old war in Bosnia which Milosevic helped start.
"Even when we celebrate our election victory, we must never forget that we have not achieved a full-scale democratisation of Serbia," Zoran Djindjic, the third leader, said.

"The main obstacle on this path is Slobodan Milosevic and his system founded on lies, monopolies and abuses. We have nothing against Milosevic and his family personally, but we want to change the system which he heads," he said.
Paris invited Zajedno leaders for talks with de Charette in a snub to Milosevic and as a signal of a policy change towards Belgrade. London promised to follow suit.
Zajedno leaders said Paris had promised assistance in running the cities where they won.

In every city where it assumed control the opposition found coffers empty and general disorder calculated to discredit it ahead of the parliamentary and presidential elections due to be held by the end of this year.

With the elections in mind Draskovic said that Zajedno had agreed to a dialogue with Milosevic on their other outstanding demands, including freeing Serbian media from state control and establishing the independence of the country's courts.

De Charette, echoing the views of other Western leaders, said Serbia's problems should be resolved by recognition of the election results, dialogue between government and opposition, free access to the media and democratic elections.
